expect:

For example: total supply voltage = 1.5 + 1.5 = 3 V; the student must calculate the series resistor needed to limit current to 20 mA — using V = I × R (with the voltage dropped across the resistor = supply voltage minus Change 'LED forward voltage ≈ 2 V if LED Vf ≈ 1 V, R = 2 ÷ 0.020 = 100 Ω' to 'LED forward voltage (Vf) for a typical red LED ≈ 2 V; voltage across resistor = 3 − 2 = 1 V; R = 1 ÷ 0.020 = 50 Ω (accept any value using a realistic Vf of 1.8–2.2 V with correct arithmetic)') — this prevents the LED from burning out (first factor, developed with calculation). Contrasted with: power consumption affects battery life — P = I × V = 0.020 × 3 = 0.06 W means the batteries will drain over time, so the student must consider capacity and efficiency in the design (second factor, developed with calculation and application to the scenario).
Secure (3–4 marks): two factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): one factor identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): a single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

find: The waveforms for these signals look very different: an analogue signal produces a smooth sine wave with a continuous range of amplitudes, while a digital signal produces a square wave that switches sharply between two voltage levels.
replace: An analogue signal varies continuously and can have different waveform shapes, including a sine wave. A digital signal can be represented by a square wave that switches between two voltage levels.
note: F5: distinguish continuous analogue variation from one possible waveform.

expect: What waveform shape does an analogue signal produce?
value: How does an analogue signal vary?
note: F5: avoid treating a sine wave as the defining analogue waveform.

expect: An analogue signal produces a smooth, continuously varying sine wave shape.
value: An analogue signal varies continuously and can have different waveform shapes, including a sine wave.
note: F5: give the correct general definition.

find: Identifying where decision diamonds create loops or branches is key to both drawing and interpreting flowcharts in the exam.
replace: For the exam, compare the advantages and disadvantages of each programming type for a given application.

find: Flowchart questions may ask you to complete, correct, or draw part of a flowchart. Always use the correct symbol shapes — drawing a process step as a diamond will lose marks. For 'compare' or 'discuss' questions about programming types, structure your answer around named advantages and disadvantages of each type, linked to the specific scenario in the question. A common mistake is describing what a flowchart looks like without explaining why the visual structure makes it easier to plan or debug a program compared with written code.
replace: For questions about programming types, explain named advantages and disadvantages and link them to the application. The specification does not require you to write or interpret programs using these systems.
note: F7: make the exam guidance match the assessed scope.

find: To find amplitude, count the vertical divisions from the lowest to highest point of the wave and multiply by the volts/div.
replace: To find the peak-to-peak voltage, count the vertical divisions from the lowest to highest point of the wave and multiply by the volts/div. For a centred sine wave, the amplitude is half this value.
note: F9: distinguish amplitude from peak-to-peak voltage.

find: A PCB production process in which a UV-sensitive coating on a copper-clad board is exposed through a mask to harden the desired track pattern, then the unwanted copper is dissolved away in an etchant chemical.
replace: A PCB production process in which a UV-sensitive coating and mask define the copper tracks to protect, then an etchant dissolves the unwanted copper.
note: F10: avoid treating negative-photoresist behaviour as universal.

find: Where the UV light reaches the photoresist it hardens (or softens, depending on whether positive or negative resist is used). Third, a developer chemical removes the unexposed (soft) photoresist, leaving the hardened photoresist protecting only the intended copper tracks.
replace: The effect of UV light depends on the photoresist type. Third, a developer removes the soluble areas, exposing the copper that will be etched while photoresist protects the intended tracks.
note: F10: describe development accurately for both resist polarities.

find: The five stages of photo etching are: (1) print photomask; (2) UV exposure — UV light hardens the photoresist over the track pattern; (3) develop — remove unexposed resist; (4) etch — dissolve unprotected copper in etchant chemical; (5) strip remaining resist to reveal copper tracks. Etchant chemicals are hazardous — proper safety precautions (gloves, goggles, neutralisation and disposal) are always required.
replace: The five stages of photo etching are: (1) print photomask; (2) UV exposure — UV light changes the photoresist pattern; (3) develop — remove the soluble resist; (4) etch — dissolve unprotected copper in etchant chemical; (5) strip remaining resist to reveal copper tracks. Etchant chemicals are hazardous — proper safety precautions (gloves, goggles, neutralisation and disposal) are always required.
note: F10: keep the process neutral about resist polarity.

expect: Description of etching stage (up to 2 marks): after development, the board is immersed in an etchant solution such as ferric chloride, which chemically dissolves the copper that is not protected by the hardened photoresist, leaving only the copper tracks beneath the resist (2 marks for a full description identifying the chemical action; 1 mark for a basic statement). Safety precaution (up to 2 marks): gloves and goggles must be worn at all times when handling etchant chemicals as they are corrosive and can cause skin and eye damage; waste etchant must be neutralised and disposed of according to local safety regulations (2 marks for a specific, developed precaution; 1 mark for a vague statement). [4 marks total]
